passage: At the Copenhagen head office Freya gave Hana the monthly sales pack on Monday, saying, “It's yours, I trust you.” On Tuesday she asked to see the draft. Hana sent it. Wednesday, Freya opened the file, changed three headings and rewrote the summary. Hana noticed the tracked changes and said nothing. Thursday, Freya asked, “Have you sent the figures to Finance yet? Show me first.” Behind the polite tone, Freya's chest was tight, because the pack carried her name upward. Hana started leaving the file half finished, waiting for Freya's edits. By Friday the pack was Freya's in every way except the name, and Hana's shoulders sagged whenever Freya walked past.

qa.q: What did Freya say when giving Hana the sales pack?
qa.a: Freya said, “It's yours, I trust you.”

qa.q: What was Freya worried about behind the tight chest and polite tone?
qa.a: Freya was anxious about accountability, since the pack carried her name upward, and the checking came from worry.

qa.q: What could Freya do differently after handing the pack over?
qa.a: Agree one checkpoint with Hana, say what standard is needed, and let Hana choose the method and send the figures.

qa.q: How might Hana see Freya's constant checks?
qa.a: Hana reads them as distrust, and stops taking ownership, waiting for the edits, which shows in the sagging shoulders.

grounding: Someone hands off work but checks every step and rewrites the output; the anxiety is about accountability, but the other person reads distrust.

passage: In the school office, Vinita, the coordinator, gave Gautam the annual day schedule to prepare. “I trust you with it,” she said. An hour later she leaned over his shoulder. “Is the timing sheet ready?” Before lunch she re-ordered the performances he had planned. In the afternoon she rewrote the announcement text and asked him to copy her version. The office clock ticked. Vinita's heart was racing whenever she thought of the principal's questions. Gautam nodded at everything, then stopped offering ideas. On the day before the event he asked Vinita, “Which one do you want me to send?” and Vinita realised, uneasily, that the schedule had stopped being Gautam's.

qa.q: What was Vinita's job in the school?
qa.a: Vinita was the coordinator in the school office.

qa.q: What was Vinita worried about when her heart raced at the thought of the principal's questions?
qa.a: Vinita was anxious about the principal's questions and felt accountable for the schedule, which drove the checking.

qa.q: What could Vinita do on the day before the event?
qa.a: Return the choice to Gautam, saying what standard is needed, and agree one final check instead of rewriting.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel when he asks which one to send?
qa.a: Gautam has probably lost confidence and feels the work is not his, and reads Vinita's edits as distrust.

grounding: Someone hands off work but checks and rewrites every step, and the other person reads distrust and stops taking ownership.

passage: Paulo had been made team lead at a design studio in Lisbon. He gave Esther, a talented junior, the task of designing a café menu. Then he checked in at ten, at noon, at three. Each time he suggested a change. On Friday she sent the final version. That night, alone in the office, Paulo moved the logo, changed two fonts and rewrote the headings. He sent his version to the client. On Monday, Esther saw it and went very quiet. The next task he gave her, she did exactly what he said, nothing more, and asked him about every small choice. Paulo felt uneasy. He had wanted her to own her work.

qa.q: What did Paulo ask Esther to design?
qa.a: A café menu.

qa.q: Why did Paulo keep checking in and rewriting the menu?
qa.a: He felt anxious about being accountable for the result, so he kept control of every detail.

qa.q: What could Paulo do differently next time?
qa.a: Agree one checkpoint and the quality expected, then let Esther deliver without quiet rewrites.

qa.q: How did Esther react to seeing her menu rewritten?
qa.a: Esther went quiet and stopped taking ownership, doing only what she was told and asking about every small choice.

grounding: Shows a lead who checks every step and quietly rewrites a junior's work, leading her to stop taking ownership.

passage: At the city school where Harsha was the new head of the science department, the annual science fair was his first big responsibility. He asked Santosh, an experienced teacher, to organise the student projects. Then he called Santosh every morning. He wanted copies of every plan. He re-did the layout of the hall without asking. The day before the fair, Santosh stopped replying to the group chat. When Harsha found him in the staffroom, Santosh said calmly, "If you want to do it yourself, tell me. I'll step back." Harsha felt his face go hot. He had been terrified of the principal's judgment, not of Santosh's skill. "I'm sorry. The fair's yours. I'll just come at the end."

qa.q: What did Harsha ask Santosh to organise?
qa.a: He asked Santosh to organise the student projects.

qa.q: What was Harsha afraid of behind the constant checking?
qa.a: He was terrified of the principal's judgment and anxious about being accountable for his first big event.

qa.q: What did Harsha do to repair things?
qa.a: He apologised, handed the fair back to Santosh, and chose to come only at the end.

qa.q: How did Santosh read Harsha's checking?
qa.a: Santosh read it as distrust and offered to step back, withdrawing from the group chat.

grounding: Shows a lead whose anxiety about accountability makes him check every step, which the teacher reads as distrust.

passage:
Dear Aparna,

I've been thinking about last month's report, and I owe you an honest note. When I gave you the donor section, I said it was yours. Then I asked for updates twice a day and rewrote your paragraphs at night without telling you. I told myself I was just polishing.

The truth is I was anxious. It was my first report as team lead, and if anything went wrong, it would be on my name.

I saw you stop suggesting ideas after the second week. I understand why. From now on: we'll agree what good looks like, meet once midway, and I won't touch your text without talking to you.

Jaya

qa.q: How often did Jaya ask Aparna for updates?
qa.a: Twice a day.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling while rewriting Aparna's paragraphs?
qa.a: Jaya felt anxious, worried that any mistake in the first report as team lead would be on Jaya's name.

qa.q: What does Jaya promise, and why could it rebuild trust?
qa.a: To agree what good looks like, meet once midway and not touch Aparna's text without talking, giving ownership back.

qa.q: How was Aparna affected by the micromanaging?
qa.a: Aparna stopped suggesting ideas after the second week, reading the checking and rewrites as distrust.

grounding: A lead's letter admits checking every step and rewriting a team member's work out of anxiety, and offers a fairer way.

passage: "People ask why my team was so quiet last season. I'm Shreya, I run wedding events at a hotel in Udaipur, and the honest answer is: me. I gave Rehana the seating plan for a four-hundred-guest wedding and said, 'It's yours.' Then I messaged her every hour. Did you separate the two uncles who don't speak? Did you check the wheelchair spaces? At night I opened her file and moved tables around without telling her. I told myself it was about the client, that if one aunty ended up by the kitchen door, my name would be on it. By the third wedding, Rehana stopped suggesting anything. She'd say, 'Just tell me what you want, ma'am.' That sentence scared me more than any client. She wasn't lazy. She'd simply learned that her work wasn't really hers."

qa.q: How many guests were at the wedding whose seating plan Shreya handed to Rehana?
qa.a: Four hundred guests.

qa.q: Why did Shreya feel she had to check every hour?
qa.a: Shreya was anxious about being blamed if anything went wrong, believing her name would be on any mistake with the client.

qa.q: What could Shreya try with the next seating plan?
qa.a: Agree one or two check-in times with Rehana, ask questions instead of silently moving tables, and let Rehana's choices stand unless something is truly wrong.

qa.q: How did the hourly messages and silent changes look from Rehana's side?
qa.a: Rehana read them as distrust, so she felt discouraged and stopped offering ideas, waiting to be told what to do.

grounding: Shows a lead who hands off work but checks every step and rewrites it out of anxiety about accountability, so the team member stops taking ownership.
